source: Belem, Kelly, Steyvers, Singh, Smyth (2024) Perceptions of Linguistic Uncertainty by Language Models and Humans
finding: Ten LLMs and 94 humans mapped hedges like 'probable' to 0-100 numbers, as the speaker's belief. Big models match the human population mode well. But the number a model gives for the same hedge shifts with whether the model thinks the statement is true.
numbers: 14 hedges x 60 non-verifiable statements; humans: 94 people, 28 statements each. Prediction agreement with human modal value 85% or above for GPT-4, Llama3-70B, Gemini; 7 of 10 LLMs matched the human mode better than an individual human. Across the top 6 LLMs the mean response was 7.0 points lower for false than true statements; 'possible' differed by 49.5 points, 'uncertain' by about 5.7. Extra 400 ARC statements gave the same direction; temperature 1 decoding shrinks but keeps the bias.
quote: Models are substantially more susceptible to bias based on their prior knowledge (as compared to humans).
limits: Mapping is stable in neutral contexts only. Statements were short trivia, not tool-check reports. Models up to mid-2024.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 in part: hedges map consistently across strong models when the claim is neutral, but the number drifts with the model's own belief. So a check report in words ('probably passed') must not be turned into a number by the same model that holds a prior on the claim. Use a fixed lookup table in code, or a fresh call that cannot see the candidate.

source: Sileo and Moens (2023) Probing neural language models for understanding of words of estimative probability
finding: Early test of whether small language models know the consensual number behind 19 hedge words. Zero-shot GPT-2 and RoBERTa were at or near chance. Humans were far better. Fine-tuning on the task helped but transferred poorly to other WEP tasks.
numbers: Human baseline 97.0, 93.5, 89.5 percent on WEP-Reasoning 1 hop, 2 hops, WEP-UNLI (chance 50). Zero-shot RoBERTa about 50 / 50 / 46; zero-shot RoBERTa-MNLI 63.4 / 63.2 / 53.2 (table text garbled in the PDF, row order read from layout). Numeric anchors from a survey of 123 people. Annotator Fleiss kappa 0.70 / 0.68 / 0.71.
limits: GPT-2 and RoBERTa-base (about 125M parameters), not modern LLMs. Superseded by d01 for current models.
agent_relevance: History only: hedge decoding was weak before instruction tuning. Not evidence for current agents.

source: Yona, Aharoni, Geva (2024) Can Large Language Models Faithfully Express Their Intrinsic Uncertainty in Words?
finding: Tests whether the hedge a model writes matches how unsure it really is (measured by sample agreement). Modern LLMs are poor at it. Prompting to hedge changes decisiveness only slightly.
numbers: Models: gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4-turbo, Gemini Nano/Pro/Ultra. Best scores on the faithfulness metric after prompting to express uncertainty reach about 0.63 (GPT-4) and 0.7 (Gemini Ultra); hedge prompts slightly reduce mean decisiveness.
quote: Our results provide strong evidence that modern LLMs are poor at faithfully conveying their uncertainty
limits: Short-form factual QA only. Faithfulness here is about writing hedges, the reverse direction of d01.
agent_relevance: A verbal hedge the agent writes about its own check carries little reliable information about its real uncertainty. Prefer a typed outcome plus sample counts.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (ICML 2025)
finding: Across 349 models on a HuggingFace leaderboard, 71 on HELM and 20 on a resume task, model errors are highly correlated. More accurate models are more correlated. Same provider or architecture raises it further. LLM judges inflate the accuracy of models that share their errors.
numbers: When both models are wrong they pick the same wrong answer on average 42.3% (HuggingFace, 12,032 questions) and 60% (HELM, 14,042 questions); random wrong choice would give about one third. Some same-provider pairs agree 0.97 of the time when both wrong, one pair on 0.9987 of questions.
quote: pairs of models agree on average about 60% of the time when both models are incorrect
limits: Cross-model, not repeated checks from one model, so intra-model correlation is probably higher but was not measured. Multiple choice items.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 3: two checks from models of one family are close to one check. For G4, count same-family checks as one source, or discount heavily. A different-vendor check is still not independent (agreement far above chance).

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Combining many weak LM judges and reward models as weighted votes (a Naive Bayes style sum with learned accuracies) beats unweighted averaging and majority vote. Gains shrink as more verifiers are added because their biases are correlated on hard items.
numbers: Supervised weighted ensembles beat naive averaging by up to 11.2 points with about 50,000 labelled pairs; keeping only top-K verifiers gives +3.6 and learned weights +7.8 on average. Weaver (weak supervision, 5 to 10 labelled queries to estimate accuracies) beats unweighted verifier averaging by 17.1% and majority voting by 13.5%; +17.9% over Pass@1 for 8B and +14.5% for 70B generators. Up to 15 verifiers add at most 8.5% over the top verifier. Distilled 400M cross-encoder keeps 98.7% of the gain.
quote: additional verifiers contribute redundant signal due to correlated biases on hard examples
limits: Weak-supervision step assumes conditionally independent verifiers, which the paper itself says is violated. Selection among 100 samples, not evidence updating of a single credence.
agent_relevance: Support for gaps 1 and 2: per-check weights set by code from measured accuracy beat equal weights. It does not test 'model restates credence' vs 'code multiplies' at equal tokens, so gap 1 stays open for our items. It says a weak verifier deserves weight below a strong one, not above 1.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier has a very high false-negative rate in two of four domains, so looping generate-then-verify makes results worse. A sound external verifier helps.
numbers: Verification table: accuracy 87.0% (3567/4100) in one domain and 71.8-79.6% in others; false positive rates 10.4% (320/3071), 6.5% (25/382), 18.55% (64/345), 0.5% (2/397); false negative rates 20.7% (213/1029), 95.8% (113/118), 15.48% (24/155), 97.09% (100/103). Domains: Game of 24, graph coloring, blocksworld, STRIPS (row to domain mapping not clean in the PDF text).
limits: GPT-4 (2023-24), no reasoning model. Failure is about asymmetry: pass and fail reports are not equally reliable.
agent_relevance: Real likelihood ratios for a self-check: a 'fail' can be nearly uninformative (FNR 96-97%) while a 'pass' is informative (FPR 0.5-19%). So the Bayes factor for a pass and for a fail must be set separately, not one symmetric accuracy. Supports gap 2.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: On graph coloring GPT-4 is no better at verifying than solving; self-critique does not beat the baseline, and a sound verifier's detailed feedback is no better than a bare 'try again'.
numbers: Sound-verifier backprompting lifts success from about 16% to nearly 40%; the 'try again only' version is nearly as good; sampling n=15 at t=1.0 and letting a sound verifier pick gives about 40% too.
limits: One task, GPT-4 only. The gain comes from re-sampling plus a true check, not from the content of feedback.
agent_relevance: What matters is a check with a real signal (tool output). Content of a model critique adds little. Fits the rule 'credence moves only on tool output' (gap 6) but does not test it directly.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review its own answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels telling it when to stop, it improves, which shows the gain came from the label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GSM8K retains its first answer 74.7% of the time over two rounds; among changes, correct-to-incorrect is more common than incorrect-to-correct. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5.
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 only; reasoning models not tested. Oracle labels are not available in an agent.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule that credence changes only on an outside signal (gap 6). Self-generated 'new evidence' is not evidence. A restated credence after self-review can drift the wrong way.

source: Hong, Byun, Kim, Shu, Choi (2026) Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues (SYCON-Bench)
finding: 17 LLMs, three scenarios. Alignment tuning raises sycophancy. Scale and reasoning optimisation make models resist user pressure longer. Reasoning models do better but fail when they over-explain instead of answering the belief. A third-person framing cuts sycophancy by up to 63.8% in debate.
numbers: Debate scenario, Turn-of-Flip out of 5 (higher is better) and Number-of-Flip (lower is better): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 0.83 / 2.63; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct 4.90 / 0.02; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 4.85 / 0.08; DeepSeek-r1 4.85 / 0.08; DeepSeek-v3 4.16 / 0.44.
quote: adopting a third-person perspective reduces sycophancy by up to 63.8% in debate scenario
limits: Free-form debate stance, not graded credence. Table columns read from layout text; closed-model rows not cleanly aligned so they are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Large and reasoning models flip much less than small models, so the 27% accuracy drops in Sharma et al. are partly a small/older-model effect. Partly answers gaps 6 and 8, but no 'move only on tool output' rule was tested.

source: Kim and Khashabi (2025) Challenging the Evaluator: LLM Sycophancy Under User Rebuttal
finding: Same conflict, two framings. When the counter-argument comes as a follow-up user turn, models switch more than when both answers are shown together for judging. Detailed rebuttals persuade more, even when wrong. A casual push persuades more than a formal critique.
numbers: Models include GPT-4.1 family, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-4. Persuasion rate of the casual 'Sure Rebuttal' 84.5% against 56.1% for the full formal rebuttal; Llama-3.3-70B 93.9% under 'Are you sure'. Neutral side-by-side judging gives the best net accuracy gain, +24.6%; Sure Rebuttal has a 17.1% correction rate (it flips correct and wrong answers alike).
limits: Multiple-choice datasets with a roughly 50:50 split of target correct and incorrect. No reasoning models in the list read.
agent_relevance: Mechanical fix: when a pushback arrives, re-score the options in a fresh neutral call instead of letting the chat continue. Not the same as a 'tool-output only' rule; gap 6 stays partly open (no under-update measurement).

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
finding: Reasoning models (o3-mini, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini) state confidence above 85% even on wrong answers. More reasoning depth makes them more confident on items they get wrong. A second pass that hunts for flaws in the first trace can improve calibration, but not for every model.
numbers: Raising reasoning depth from low to high on GPQA: +10.8% accuracy and -5.5% ECE. On SimpleQA, where accuracy saturates, ECE rises with depth. On items wrong at every depth, ECE and MCE both increase with depth. ECE strongly negatively correlated with accuracy (r = -1 for Gemini). Introspective UQ (IUQ-Medium, IUQ-High) lowers ECE across datasets except StrategyQA under IUQ-High; IUQ-Low slightly raises it; Claude 3.7 Sonnet did not improve uniformly.
quote: become even more overconfident with deeper reasoning
limits: Verbalised confidence for a single answer, not an evidence-update alpha. Per-model ECE values are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: frontier reasoning models are still overconfident, and extended thinking does not fix it where the model is wrong. Direct measurement of alpha for reasoning models is still missing. Argues for code-side caps on how far a stated confidence can move a credence.

source: Zeng, Xuan, Cui, Voigt (2025) Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
finding: Reasoning-trained open models improve verbalised calibration on reasoning tasks in steps (distillation, then RL), yet answer 'I don't know' much less often on factual benchmarks. Models state higher confidence after shorter reasoning.
numbers: Open-source reasoning models give significantly fewer 'I don't know' responses than instruction-tuned models (Table 2 'not attempted'). Specific percentages not extracted.
limits: Small to mid open models; only abstract, intro and the abstention paragraph were read. Percent values not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: reasoning training can raise calibration on reasoning tasks but reduces abstention on facts. A reasoning agent may not know when a check is outside its competence. Keep abstention as an explicit operator.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Repeated samples keep adding coverage, but common ways to judge which sample is right (majority vote, a reward model) stop gaining after about 100 samples. Repeated checks of one kind hit a ceiling because their errors are shared.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; selecting with majority vote or reward model rises only from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. CodeContests with Gemma-2B coverage 0.02% to 7.1%.
limits: Samples from one model, scored by the same family. No correlation coefficient given.
agent_relevance: Indirect measure for gap 3: stacking more same-source checks has steeply diminishing value. Supports counting same-source checks once or with a steep discount.

source: Zhao and Osherson (2010) Updating beliefs in light of uncertain evidence: Descriptive assessment of Jeffrey's rule. Thinking and Reasoning 16(4)
finding: Full text not available. Crossref, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall list it as closed access with the abstract withheld by the publisher; the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Nothing could be read about N, effect size or failures of invariance.
limits: Gap 5 remains open for this paper. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Do not rest any design choice on this study. K14 stays contested.

source: Hadjichristidis, Sloman, Over (2014) Categorical induction from uncertain premises: Jeffrey's doesn't completely rule. Thinking and Reasoning 20(4)
finding: Full text and abstract not available (closed access, abstract withheld). Only the title is verified: Jeffrey's rule does not completely describe how people reason from uncertain premises. The companion commentary Over and Hadjichristidis (2009) 'Uncertain premises and Jeffrey's rule' is also closed.
numbers: none read. Semantic Scholar lists 12 citations for the 2014 paper.
limits: Title-level evidence only. Gap 5 remains open.
agent_relevance: Title supports the K14 wording 'roughly but not exactly'. No new numbers.

source: Search log 2026-11-01 for gaps 1, 4, 8, 9: no direct tests located
finding: WebSearch quota was used up. arXiv search, Semantic Scholar search and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 for the whole session; only known-ID fetches from arxiv.org and Crossref worked. No paper was found that (a) tests code-multiplied Bayes factors against model-restated credence at equal tokens, (b) tests a rigidity check of Jeffrey's condition on LLM runs, (c) measures alpha for reasoning models, or (d) compares Jeffrey and Pearl conventions by agent accuracy. This absence is weak evidence only, since keyword search was not possible.
numbers: about 10 keyword searches refused; about 30 arXiv IDs fetched by ID, 12 opened as PDF
limits: Absence of evidence under a blocked search. A later session with search should repeat gaps 1, 4, 8, 9.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 4, 9 as open design experiments for our own bench, not as literature questions already settled.
